title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 188
paragraphs: Now when Cyrus on his way toward Babylon arrived at the river Gyndes — whose springs are in the mountains of the Matienians, and which flows through the Dardanians and runs into another river, the Tigris, which, flowing by the city of Opis, runs out into the Erythraian Sea — when Cyrus, I say, was attempting to cross this river Gyndes, which is a navigable stream, then one of his sacred white horses, in high spirit and wantonness, went into the river and tried to cross, but the stream swept it under water and carried it off at once. Cyrus was greatly moved with anger against the river for having acted so insolently, and he threatened to make it so feeble that for the future even women could cross it easily without wetting the knee. So after this threat he ceased from his march against Babylon and divided his army into two parts; and having divided it, he stretched lines and marked out straight channels, one hundred and eighty on each bank of the Gyndes, directed every way, and having disposed his army along them he commanded them to dig. So, as a great multitude was working, the work was indeed completed, but they spent the whole summer season at this spot working.
